comment: Minimum PASSING test count per workspace, checked by scripts/check-test-floor.mjs. This is a RATCHET against a suite that silently shrinks, not a coverage target. It exists because `--experimental-test-isolation=none` (see .github/workflows/ci.yml) swallows a module-level throw once any test in that file has registered: the run goes green, exits 0, and simply reports fewer tests. Measured: 2174 instead of 2175, with `# fail 0`. A count floor is the only thing that turns that back into a red. Raise these when tests are added; lowering one is a deliberate act that should be explained in the commit. LOWERED 2026-08-19: backthread 729 -> 714 (712 after the removal, +3 for the retired-name tests: two behavioural, one over its source). The pre-edit PreToolUse hook was removed (founder decision, see cli/hooks/hooks.json's $comment_no_pretooluse_edit), retiring editNudge.test.ts's 15 tests and 2 `edit-context` dispatch tests in bin.test.ts. The suite shrank because the feature did, not because tests were dropped: the case that pinned the hook's existence was INVERTED into a guard in plugin.test.ts rather than deleted. RAISED 2026-08-21: backthread 715 -> 847 (+132), measured, for the failure-copy work. Nothing was removed: src/failureCopy.test.ts is new (the renderer, the endpoint registry, the guards, and a conformance battery of 4 properties x 9 rendered endpoints generated FROM the registry, so the count moves with the endpoint list), plus flag-dispatch cases in bin.test.ts and behavioural cases added to capture/infer/inflow/lesson/localDecisions/onboardingState tests. Several EXISTING tests changed their expected string rather than being dropped, because the rendered failure changed, which is the point of the change. The number rose across four rounds as three independent reviews each found real defects: two registry entries claiming a failure was never shown on surfaces that print it, the renderer treating `error` as always a machine slug when the worker also writes prose there, a bug-report tail appended to deliberate refusals, seven ways past the endpoint guard, and five surviving mutants. A fourth review then found a prototype-chain leak putting `function toString() { [native code] }` in front of a user, two copy entries advising the reader to ask owners of a repo that by definition has none, an instruction the MCP surface could not follow, six more ways past the endpoint guard, and nine survivors. A fifth review then found raw Postgres text still reaching a reader through the `error` field on Edge-Function 500s, four sentences wrong about the condition they fire on, three entries no reachable route sends, three more guard escapes, and thirteen survivors. The copy is now asserted SENTENCE BY SENTENCE rather than by length, because copy is the product here. A sixth review found the endpoint guard still passable by two ordinary spellings — an origin routed through a private helper, and one function that both built a URL and fetched it — while three shipped claims said it was not. Endpoints can now be born in exactly one module, that module is forbidden to make requests, and every export of it must be registered, and no request may be pointed at a URL that was invented or edited rather than built there. A seventh review found five more spellings past the previous version — surgery on a builder's result, a hardcoded host, a name-shaped exemption, an `export { }` list, and an origin interpolated in front of a path that the guard's own comment-stripper had erased before it looked. The stripper is a scanner now, because a regex pair ate from the `//` inside every URL string it was meant to find. Every one of those is a named test.  RAISED 2026-08-19: @backthread/extractor 2175 -> 2201 for packages/extractor/src/safety.test.ts — the source-tree budget and its symlink-escape guard, which previously had no test that failed when it broke. RAISED 2026-08-21: backthread 847 -> 865 (+18), measured, for the shell-command path harvest. Nothing was removed: the harvest that reads file paths out of Bash/shell command strings is new, and so is the gate that only emits a path the file actually exists in the working tree. An independent review then fuzzed it with 4,000 hostile commands and found real leaks the string rules could not catch -- a file reached after `cd` out of the repo, a scheme-less URL's hostname and route, string literals inside a heredoc, .git/ and node_modules/, a 16,892-character token and a command yielding 20,000 paths -- so the count also covers a named test per hostile input plus the two caps. Two claims the code did not honour were corrected rather than re-asserted: the extension list's longest-first sort was dead code (the trailing lookahead does that work) and the lookbehind was not what kept URLs out (the repo-root fence was). Tests now assert WHICH gate rejected a token, so a case cannot pass because a different rule happened to catch it.  RAISED 2026-08-29: backthread 865 -> 924 (+59), measured, for the containment-fence hardening. Nothing was removed. The additions are: six cases on the path fence itself (a caller-reported escape dropping a path from BOTH the tool-input and the shell route, the same caller reporting no escape leaving every path untouched, a dropped path not spending the shell budget, and a NUL byte refused from every origin); an end-to-end case built on real git repos, a real symlink out of the checkout and real files, which pins the two halves of the rule at once -- a path descending THROUGH a link into another repository is dropped, while this repo own name for a file that happens to be a link out is kept; and captureNotice.test.ts, which is new, covering the file capture leaves behind when it has something to say, because the shipped hook discards its own stdio and had no other channel. Two capture cases pin that the sentence reaches both stderr and that file, and one drives it end to end into the `backthread doctor` report. Three more came from an independent verification round: the cap boundary at 63/64/65 (a surviving mutant fired the notice at exactly the cap, announcing "the other 0"), and two end-to-end cases for a directory reached through a symlinked PARENT -- one a git checkout, one not a repo at all. The second is what makes resolving the root set load-bearing rather than defensive: with no git there the root set is the session cwd alone, carrying the symlinked spelling and no physical counterpart, so comparing a resolved path against the unresolved roots matches nothing and every path reads as having left a repo that does not exist. That mutant survived until this case existed. Five more came from an independent code review that found two live leaks the first round did not close. A sibling worktree could VOUCH for an escaping link: roots are checkouts of one repo, so every tracked directory exists in all of them, and a rule that kept a path as soon as some root resolved it inside let the sibling launder an escape at a name the repo genuinely has. And a link into a MISSING directory resolved nowhere, which read as an absence rather than a contradiction, so the same link leaked or did not purely by what sat on its far side. One case each, end to end on real repos and real links, plus the deleted-file property re-asserted inside the second so the ancestor climb cannot quietly take it away. Then prunable worktree registrations, which git still lists and which were spending capped verification slots and inflating the count reported to the reader -- two cases, one for the skip and one for the annotation not bleeding into the records after it. And isInsideRoot, which is exported with an injected separator ONLY so the win32 spelling can be exercised: realpath and join answer in the platform separator, a hardcoded slash makes every path below a root read as an escape there, and no test running on this machine can tell sep from a slash. That mutant survived an end-to-end test and dies against this one. Three more close claims that were written in comments and guarded by nothing, found by mutating them: the escape check being handed the roots the harvest ACTUALLY used rather than the caller list (it falls back to a root found in the transcript, and a predicate closed over the caller empty list can only ever answer no-escape), and the two doctor lines -- an absent notice must report the state of the mailbox and claim nothing about a capture that may never have happened, and a notice must warn with its date without ever driving the exit code.  RAISED 2026-08-29: backthread 924 -> 929 (+5), measured, for resolving a harvested path against the filesystem BEFORE normalizing it. Nothing was removed. The previous fence resolved the path it was about to EMIT, and two mechanisms walked through that: a `..` cancelled arithmetically against a SYMLINKED segment reduces to a name this repo genuinely has while the kernel opens another repository's file, and a segment whose realpath FAILS was climbed past to the nearest ancestor that resolved, which lands back inside the repo -- measured for a dangling link, for an escaping link behind a chmod-000 directory, and for a symlink loop. The additions are: one end-to-end case on real git repos, real symlinks and real files carrying 23 distinct re-spellings of an escape, each aimed at a DISTINCT file so one leak cannot be mistaken for another, asserting the four properties that must survive it and that not one machine-absolute path is emitted; one case pinning the seam that separates positive absence (ENOENT, the deleted file, which keeps its path) from a filesystem that will not answer (which must not); one for the walk-depth cap failing CLOSED rather than open; one pinning that the RAW spelling crosses the package boundary while the normalized one is still what gets emitted, because a half-resolved path crossing that boundary is the defect; and one refusing URI schemes and percent-escaped separators, which is where a machine-absolute path was leaving. The `..` cases needed a link that stays INSIDE the repo with the `..` after it doing the leaving -- every earlier fixture had the link itself land outside, so a mutant that skipped `..` entirely survived until that case existed. The fifth pins the trade-off that comes with resolving a place instead of judging a name: an honest file in a sibling checkout, at a name the primary checkout links out of, is dropped when it is spelled RELATIVELY (a name is all that spelling gives, and any root saying the name leaves is enough) and recovered when it is spelled ABSOLUTELY (that is a place, it can be followed on its own, and no root gets to vouch for it) -- while the escape through the very same name is refused in both spellings. Either half alone reads as a bug, so the pair is one test.  RAISED 2026-08-29: backthread 930 -> 931 (+1, plus two spellings and a cat assertion added to the existing end-to-end case), for two defects an independent verification round found in the first version of the above. A FILENAME CONTAINING A BACKSLASH escaped: this module treated `\` as a second path separator so a Windows spelling could be normalized like a POSIX one, but on POSIX `\` is an ordinary filename character -- so a symlink genuinely NAMED `x\y`, pointing at another repository, was read by the fence as two segments that do not exist, called empty ground inside the repo, and kept, while the kernel resolved it in one hop into the other repo. Proven by reading the file through that spelling. It is the same defect as `..` cancelled on the string wearing a different costume: the fence measuring a DIFFERENT PATH from the one that gets opened. There is no reading of `\` correct on both platforms and this module cannot know which produced the string, so a path carrying one is now refused outright and `/` is the only separator anywhere below that line. AND AN UNRESOLVABLE ROOT could vouch: the resolved-root set drops a root that no longer resolves, the code says so in a comment, and nothing could fail on it -- keeping the logical spelling beside physical ones lets a deleted, renamed or unmounted directory confirm paths by prefix. Two roots, one live and one gone, with the live root's own file asserted alongside so a green cannot mean nothing was sent. The same round also had the NUL refusal widened to every C0 control character, because a transcript-supplied string containing a newline was reaching the wire as a "path" that renders as two lines.
